Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] curl.exe downloading MSI payload into ProgramData (msaRAT delivery)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Don’t swing at everything
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] msiexec executing MSI masquerading as Windows update from ProgramData · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Chrome/Edge launched with --remote-debugging-port by non-browser parent (CDP abuse) · [LLM] Plain-HTTP over port 443 to msaRAT delivery IP 172.86.126.18 · [LLM] Browser contacting msaRAT WebRTC signaling relay (workers.dev Cloudflare Worker) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
curl.exe downloading MSI payload into ProgramData (msaRAT delivery) AIDelivery High
Hunts msaRAT's initial delivery step where curl.exe pulls an MSI impersonating a Windows update into C:\ProgramData over plain HTTP. Article-specific because it pairs the curl LOLBin with both a .msi extension and a ProgramData drop path — Talos explicitly flags this exact command shape. Rationale: Uses the exact Talos-described command shape (curl + .msi + ProgramData). Two independent sources (BleepingComputer, The Hacker News) confirm curl.exe pulls the MSI into ProgramData, making this high-fidelity rather than a generic ingress-tool-transfer template. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Software packaging/deployment tooling using curl to stage MSI installers in ProgramData
  • IT admin manually downloading a vendor MSI to a ProgramData staging folder
  • RMM/patch-management agents (e.g. Chocolatey, PDQ) that fetch MSIs via curl
  • CI/build agents that pull MSI artifacts into ProgramData for testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pdqdeployrunner.exe","choco.exe","chocolatey.exe","ninite.exe","tacticalrmm.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full curl command line and the source URL/IP; confirm whether the host has legitimate deployment tooling that uses curl, and check the SHA256 of the dropped MSI against Talos IOCs. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the source IP (172.86.126.18) at the firewall, and quarantine the MSI in ProgramData before it is executed by msiexec. 3) Hunt: search the host and peers for subsequent msiexec.exe execution of the ProgramData MSI, chrome.exe/msedge.exe launched with --remote-debugging-port, and outbound connections to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ProgramData"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".msi" and CommandLine has "ProgramData"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: curl.exe Downloading MSI to ProgramData (msaRAT delivery)

| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
msiexec executing MSI masquerading as Windows update from ProgramData AIInstallation High
Hunts msaRAT's execution step: msiexec launching a curl-dropped MSI from ProgramData whose name impersonates a Windows update/patch, whose install runs a custom action loading a DLL from inside the installer straight into memory. Article-specific via the ProgramData path plus update/patch/KB naming lure. Rationale: Anchors on the confirmed masquerade (MSI posing as a Windows update dropped in ProgramData) reported by Talos and echoed by The Hacker News. Legitimate Windows updates never install from ProgramData via a curl-dropped MSI, so the path+name combination is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party app updaters that stage MSIs in a vendor ProgramData subfolder with 'update' in the name
  • Enterprise patch tooling repackaging updates as MSIs staged in ProgramData
  • Driver/firmware update MSIs (e.g. Dell/HP) named with 'update' running from ProgramData
  • Internal software distribution that names MSIs after KB numbers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pdqdeployrunner.exe","choco.exe","tacticalrmm.exe","dellcommandupdate.exe","hpsupportassistant.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the MSI path/name and its SHA256, and identify the parent process — a curl.exe or unknown ProgramData binary parent is a strong TP signal. 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill/quarantine the msiexec chain; snapshot memory since the custom action loads a DLL directly into memory. 3) Hunt: look for the browser being launched with --remote-debugging-port shortly after, connections to 172.86.126.18:443 and is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev, and stage for possible ransomware pre-encryption behavior.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ProgramData"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","patch","windows","KB")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "ProgramData" and CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has_any ("update","patch","windows","KB")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Msiexec Running Windows-Update-Themed MSI from ProgramData

Chrome/Edge launched with --remote-debugging-port by non-browser parent (CDP abuse) AICommand & Control High
Hunts msaRAT driving Chrome or Edge over the Chrome DevTools Protocol by starting the browser with a --remote-debugging-port flag, typically spawned by the malicious loader rather than a user shell. This is the core living-off-the-browser C2 setup Talos describes. Rationale: Talos and multiple write-ups (BleepingComputer, Gridinsoft) confirm msaRAT starts a headless browser and drives it via CDP; the --remote-debugging-port flag is the observable that enables CDP. Excluding legit browser/explorer parents removes the bulk of benign automation while keeping the loader-spawned case. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/msarat-chrome-edge-browser-c2/
ATT&CKT1205 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated browser testing frameworks (Selenium, Puppeteer, Playwright) launching Chrome with a debug port
  • Developers manually debugging web apps with remote debugging enabled
  • Electron/CEF-based apps that invoke chromium with a debugging port
  • Headless-Chrome PDF/screenshot rendering services spawned by app servers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","selenium.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe","pwsh.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "puppeteer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "playwright"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and its folder path — a parent from ProgramData or an unsigned/unknown binary is a strong TP; check for a co-occurring loopback (127.0.0.1) CDP connection. 2) Contain: isolate the host and terminate the parent loader plus the debug-port browser instance. 3) Hunt: correlate with the same host reaching is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev (WebRTC signaling) and Twilio TURN, and look back for the curl→MSI→msiexec delivery chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","code.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "\\explorer.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\chrome.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Browser Started with Remote Debugging Port by Non-Browser Parent (msaRAT CDP)

Plain-HTTP over port 443 to msaRAT delivery IP 172.86.126.18 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts msaRAT's evasive delivery channel: unencrypted HTTP to the confirmed C2/staging IP 172.86.126.18 on port 443, which slips past firewalls that trust 443 by number without protocol inspection. Anchored on the confirmed network IOC plus the plaintext-on-443 behavior Talos calls out. Rationale: 172.86.126.18:443 is a confirmed IOC (Talos IOC table, echoed by Help Net Security). Talos specifically notes the traffic is plain HTTP on 443 to bypass port-only firewall rules, so pairing the exact IP with port 443 (and HttpConnectionInspected on 443 as the plaintext behavior) is high-confidence and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195876/malware/chaos-ransomware-deploys-browser-based-msarat-to-evade-network-detection.html
ATT&CKT1572 T1090.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • If the IP is later reassigned to a benign hosting tenant, unrelated legitimate traffic could hit it
  • Security scanners/threat-intel validation tooling deliberately probing the IOC IP
  • Proxy or gateway appliances logging the connection on behalf of many hosts (source attribution noise)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process (curl.exe or a ProgramData binary is a strong TP) and whether the payload on 443 was HTTP rather than TLS. 2) Contain: block 172.86.126.18 org-wide at egress, isolate any host that connected, and preserve the downloaded MSI. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same hosts for browser --remote-debugging-port launches and DNS/connections to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev, and sweep the environment for other hosts touching this IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18"
| where RemotePort == 443 or ActionType == "HttpConnectionInspected"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "172.86.126.18" and DestinationPort == 443
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser contacting msaRAT WebRTC signaling relay (workers.dev Cloudflare Worker) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the msaRAT C2 signaling stage where the hijacked Chrome/Edge browser performs SDP offer/answer exchange with the Cloudflare Worker is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev before opening a WebRTC data channel via Twilio TURN. Anchored on the confirmed signaling-relay domain IOC. Rationale: is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev is the confirmed signaling-relay IOC (Talos IOC table, corroborated by Help Net Security/Security Affairs describing SDP exchange with a Cloudflare Worker). A resolution/connection to this exact FQDN is a direct C2 hit; the WebRTC channel itself (Twilio TURN/UDP 3478) is too noisy to detect standalone, so this domain is the reliable pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195876/malware/chaos-ransomware-deploys-browser-based-msarat-to-evade-network-detection.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1205
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • If the specific Worker subdomain is sinkholed/reassigned, benign scanner traffic could hit it
  • Threat-intel or DFIR tooling deliberately resolving the IOC domain during validation
  • Web proxy logging the lookup on behalf of many clients, obscuring the true source host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which process resolved/connected to the domain — a browser process (chrome.exe/msedge.exe) driven via CDP is the expected msaRAT pattern. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block *.ols-img-12.workers.dev (and the exact FQDN) at DNS/egress, isolate the host, and terminate the browser instance carrying the WebRTC channel. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host for --remote-debugging-port browser launches, 127.0.0.1 CDP loopback traffic, connections to 172.86.126.18:443, and the upstream curl→MSI delivery; check for staged ransomware activity.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort),
(DeviceEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
 | where RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl)
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.execution
logsource:

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FakeAgent: ClaudeDesktop.exe execution + tampered libcef.dll side-load (SectopRAT) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: Android Spyware, PLC Attacks, AI Image Prompt Injection + 12 More St
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm postinstall dropper spawns osascript (AMOS macOS stealer via @copilot-mcp/apex) · [LLM] FakeAgent SectopRAT persistence: DockerDesktop.exe scheduled task + Defender exclusion · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AMOS stealer exfil staging /tmp/osalogging.zip + LaunchAgent C2 persistence (macOS) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
npm postinstall dropper spawns osascript (AMOS macOS stealer via @copilot-mcp/apex) AIInstallation High
Hunts a Node/npm process tree spawning osascript on macOS, the exact second-stage behaviour of the @copilot-mcp/apex and @apexfdn/apex droppers that decrypt and run an AMOS-family AppleScript payload. Legitimate npm installs almost never spawn osascript, making the parent→child pair high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated chain (npm install/npx @copilot-mcp/apex -> osascript AppleScript payload). Corroborated by Microsoft and SOC Prime macOS-stealer write-ups that flag node->osascript as the AMOS delivery signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/02/infostealers-without-borders-macos-python-stealers-and-platform-abuse/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/macos-stealers-observed-what-defenders-should-watch-for/
ATT&CKT1059.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate npm package that uses osascript to prompt for permissions during postinstall (rare, e.g. some GUI-integration tooling)
  • Developer manually testing an AppleScript build step from a Node script
  • Electron/Node tooling that shells out to osascript to display native macOS notifications
  • Homebrew Node formula post-install scripts invoking osascript for UI
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","npx","@copilot-mcp/apex","@apexfdn/apex") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("decrypt","base64","do shell script","curl","osalogging")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full osascript command line and the initiating npm/npx command; look for base64, gunzip, curl, JXA, or a decrypt routine in the AppleScript body and check for a package name matching @copilot-mcp/apex or @apexfdn/apex. 2) Contain: isolate the macOS host, kill the osascript/node chain, and revoke any AWS/Kubernetes/SSH creds and browser/crypto-wallet secrets that were on-disk (this stealer harvests them). 3) Hunt: search the same host and package registry usage across the fleet for /tmp/osalogging.zip and LaunchAgents polling a C2, and audit which developers ran that package.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "osascript"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","npx","node.js") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npx ","postinstall","@copilot-mcp/apex","@apexfdn/apex")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "osascript"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","npx","node.js") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npx ","postinstall","@copilot-mcp/apex","@apexfdn/apex")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AMOS stealer exfil staging /tmp/osalogging.zip + LaunchAgent C2 persistence (macOS) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts creation of the AMOS stealer's fixed exfil archive /tmp/osalogging.zip and/or a LaunchAgent plist written alongside osascript/curl activity that polls the C2 every 60 seconds. These are hardcoded artefacts of the @copilot-mcp/apex payload, giving a near-zero-FP alert. Rationale: Uses two fixed article strings: the /tmp/osalogging.zip staging archive and the LaunchAgent that polls C2 every 60s. The zip path is a literal, near-unique IOC; the LaunchAgent+osascript pairing is corroborated by Microsoft/SOC Prime AMOS persistence analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://socprime.com/active-threats/macos-stealers-observed-what-defenders-should-watch-for/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/02/infostealers-without-borders-macos-python-stealers-and-platform-abuse/
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1543.001 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or backup tool coincidentally naming a zip 'osalogging.zip' (extremely unlikely)
  • Legitimate app writing a LaunchAgent that shells out to curl for update checks
  • Corporate MDM deploying a LaunchAgent for telemetry (whitelist the MDM signing process)
  • Security tooling itself staging archives in /tmp during testing
Suppression filter
| where FileName =~ "osalogging.zip" or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "osascript" and FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (should be osascript or a Node-descended shell); pull the LaunchAgent plist and read its ProgramArguments for the C2 URL and 60s polling loop. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the LaunchAgent and quarantine the payload, and force-rotate every credential class the stealer targets (browser, 20+ crypto wallets, SSH, AWS, Kubernetes, login Keychain, Telegram). 3) Hunt: pivot on the C2 host from the plist across DNS/proxy logs, and sweep for node->osascript execution (see companion UC) to find the initial dropper.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "osalogging.zip")
    or (FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" and ActionType == "FileCreated" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("osascript","curl","/tmp/"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "osalogging.zip")
    or (FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" and ActionType == "FileCreated" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("osascript","curl","/tmp/"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FakeAgent: ClaudeDesktop.exe execution + tampered libcef.dll side-load (SectopRAT) AIDelivery High
Hunts the FakeAgent malvertising payload — a fake ClaudeDesktop.exe downloaded from an attacker site (via a Claude.ai artifact redirect) that runs a renamed signed JetBrains binary to side-load a tampered libcef.dll carrying SectopRAT. Targets both the named lure binary and the DLL-sideload-from-staging-dir behaviour. Rationale: ClaudeDesktop.exe is the article's named lure binary (the genuine app ships as Claude.exe). Huntress corroboration adds the tampered libcef.dll side-load loaded from a user-writable staging dir, which the DeviceImageLoadEvents leg catches even if the lure binary is renamed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/anthropic-claude-artifacts-download-malware/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1204.002 T1583.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Claude desktop app (ships as Claude.exe, not ClaudeDesktop.exe) — name mismatch keeps FP low
  • Legitimate CEF/Electron apps (Spotify, Steam, portable browsers) loading libcef.dll from install dirs — excluded by the staging-dir path filter
  • A portable/dev build of a real app run from Downloads that legitimately carries libcef.dll
  • Internal software repackaging that stages CEF apps in Temp during MSI extraction
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and Signal == "libcef.dll side-load from staging dir")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the ClaudeDesktop.exe path/hash against the genuine Claude.exe; inspect the process that loaded libcef.dll for a valid JetBrains signature but an out-of-place folder (Downloads/Temp), and check for VMProtect packing and a GPU/graphics-hardware check (anti-VM). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, quarantine the ClaudeDesktop.exe bundle and tampered libcef.dll, and block the attacker download domain. 3) Hunt: pivot to the companion DockerDesktop.exe scheduled-task/Defender-exclusion UC, review Bing/ad-referred downloads across the fleet, and check for SectopRAT credit-card/credential exfil beacons.
let ClaudeLure = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "ClaudeDesktop.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="ClaudeDesktop.exe execution", Path=FolderPath, Cmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
let LibcefSideload = DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "libcef.dll"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="libcef.dll side-load from staging dir", Path=FolderPath, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256=InitiatingProcessSHA256;
union ClaudeLure, LibcefSideload
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\ClaudeDesktop.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FakeAgent SectopRAT persistence: DockerDesktop.exe scheduled task + Defender exclusion AIInstallation High
Hunts the FakeAgent post-exploitation persistence — a dropped DockerDesktop.exe registered as a scheduled task, plus Add-MpPreference Defender exclusions the operator sets to protect the payload. Both are hardcoded behaviours Huntress observed across the 29 victim organizations. Rationale: DockerDesktop.exe as a scheduled-task persistence binary (genuine Docker Desktop ships as 'Docker Desktop.exe' with a space, in Program Files) plus Add-MpPreference exclusions are the two persistence/evasion steps Huntress documented for FakeAgent; both are user-context, non-machine-account actions. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat • https://www.itsecurityguru.org/2026/07/23/fakeagent-campaign-malicious-claude-artifact-used-to-distribute-sectoprat-to-29-organisations/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Docker Desktop install task ('Docker Desktop.exe' with space, under Program Files) — the no-space DockerDesktop.exe token reduces overlap
  • Endpoint/AV admin legitimately adding a Defender exclusion via Add-MpPreference during troubleshooting
  • EDR or software-deployment tooling registering scheduled tasks under SYSTEM (filtered by machine-account exclusion)
  • A developer scripting Register-ScheduledTask for a personal automation named 'Docker...'
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("gpscript.exe","msiexec.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has @"\Program Files\Docker\Docker\Docker Desktop.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the scheduled-task action path/hash for DockerDesktop.exe (confirm it's in a user-writable dir, not Program Files) and enumerate any Defender exclusions added around the same time (Get-MpPreference) to see what the operator is protecting. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the rogue task, remove the exclusion, and quarantine DockerDesktop.exe and the associated ClaudeDesktop.exe/libcef.dll bundle. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same DockerDesktop.exe task name and identical exclusion paths, and correlate to the FakeAgent delivery UC (ClaudeDesktop.exe / libcef.dll side-load).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("/create","DockerDesktop.exe"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("Register-ScheduledTask","DockerDesktop"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-ExclusionPath","-ExclusionProcess"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has "DockerDesktop.exe")
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and CommandLine has_any ("-ExclusionPath","-ExclusionProcess"))
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask" and CommandLine has "DockerDesktop")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FakeAgent SectopRAT persistence via DockerDesktop.exe task or Defender exclusion
id: c81f5a67-2b90-4e13-8d6c-9f0a4b7e5d22
description: Detects the FakeAgent campaign persistence steps - registering a dropped DockerDesktop.exe as a scheduled task or adding a Microsoft Defender exclusion via Add-MpPreference
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-android-spyware-plc-attacks.html
  - https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1562.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  sel_task:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/create'
      - 'DockerDesktop.exe'
  sel_defender:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'Add-MpPreference'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-ExclusionPath'
      - '-ExclusionProcess'
  condition: sel_task or sel_defender
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 ((@Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*DockerDesktop.exe* AND */create*)) OR (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) AND @CommandLine:*Add-MpPreference* AND @CommandLine:(*-ExclusionPath* OR *-ExclusionProcess*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i CommandLine=/\/create/i CommandLine=/DockerDesktop\.exe/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i CommandLine=/Add-MpPreference/i CommandLine=/(ExclusionPath|ExclusionProcess)/i)
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe AND Processes.process="*DockerDesktop.exe*" AND Processes.process="*/create*") OR (Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe,pwsh.exe) AND Processes.process="*Add-MpPreference*" AND Processes.process="*Exclusion*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe AND Processes.process="*DockerDesktop.exe*" AND Processes.process="*/create*") OR (Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe,pwsh.exe) AND Processes.process="*Add-MpPreference*" AND Processes.process="*Exclusion*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20

    by src, second_level_domain

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when

references:

detection:

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'

            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ecd1113fae1ede9869afd9d1af612bab7f1a2054e5c45a346e18c107c22b9164", "233f90180b529aa32911901e5222e9ed9c3cd24c", "3b9a880ae4e1c5b7bbd68e118a1c3c8b592f7bfb") or SHA1 in~ ("ecd1113fae1ede9869afd9d1af612bab7f1a2054e5c45a346e18c107c22b9164", "233f90180b529aa32911901e5222e9ed9c3cd24c", "3b9a880ae4e1c5b7bbd68e118a1c3c8b592f7bfb") or MD5 in~ ("ecd1113fae1ede9869afd9d1af612bab7f1a2054e5c45a346e18c107c22b9164", "233f90180b529aa32911901e5222e9ed9c3cd24c", "3b9a880ae4e1c5b7bbd68e118a1c3c8b592f7bfb")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ecd1113fae1ede9869afd9d1af612bab7f1a2054e5c45a346e18c107c22b9164", "233f90180b529aa32911901e5222e9ed9c3cd24c", "3b9a880ae4e1c5b7bbd68e118a1c3c8b592f7bfb") or SHA1 in~ ("ecd1113fae1ede9869afd9d1af612bab7f1a2054e5c45a346e18c107c22b9164", "233f90180b529aa32911901e5222e9ed9c3cd24c", "3b9a880ae4e1c5b7bbd68e118a1c3c8b592f7bfb") or MD5 in~ ("ecd1113fae1ede9869afd9d1af612bab7f1a2054e5c45a346e18c107c22b9164", "233f90180b529aa32911901e5222e9ed9c3cd24c", "3b9a880ae4e1c5b7bbd68e118a1c3c8b592f7bfb")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ecd1113fae1ede9869afd9d1af612bab7f1a2054e5c45a346e18c107c22b9164", "233f90180b529aa32911901e5222e9ed9c3cd24c", "3b9a880ae4e1c5b7bbd68e118a1c3c8b592f7bfb"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-23 14 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

In the second quarter of 2026, the continuing effects of Microsoft’s disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing platform contributed to sustained declines in several major phishing techniques, while threat actors expanded into Teams-based social engineering and employed increasingly automated and multi-stage attack chains. The post Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound malware campaign email from DKIM-signed sender 9i6pokerdepot.com · [LLM] Second-stage BAT dropper retrieval from ClickUp attachment subdomain t90141296286 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BAT-spawned hidden PowerShell pulling installer from pixeldrain.com · [LLM] LOLBin download of installer.exe from pixeldrain.com API to user Temp · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Inbound malware campaign email from DKIM-signed sender 9i6pokerdepot.com AIDelivery High
Hunts the specific Q2 2026 automated malware-delivery campaign that abused a DKIM-signing sending domain (9i6pokerdepot.com / Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com) and addressed generic role-based mailboxes to deliver a nested-EML + calendar-invite lure. Anchors on the exact operator sender identity rather than generic phishing heuristics. Rationale: Sender domain/address 9i6pokerdepot.com and Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com are from the article IOC table (first/last seen 2026-06-15). External write-up confirmed the campaign targeted role-based mailboxes (ar, accountsreceivable, hr, payroll) and used a login.microsoftonline.com auth-redirect lure, making the sender identity a high-fidelity anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate business partner legitimately registers a lookalike gambling/finance domain (extremely unlikely for this exact string)
  • Security team replaying the phishing sample into a test tenant
  • Threat-intel/phish-simulation vendor sending a controlled test from a spoofed address
  • Internal forwarding of the original malicious mail as an attachment for reporting
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryLocation !in ("Quarantine","Blocked")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all EmailEvents for SenderFromDomain 9i6pokerdepot.com, note DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation and whether any landed in Inbox vs quarantined; expand EmailAttachmentInfo for nested .eml/.ics. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge delivered copies via Explorer, block the sender domain and Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com at the mail gateway, and check UrlClickEvents for any recipient clicks. 3) Hunt: for any clicker, pivot to the ClickUp/pixeldrain UCs below to confirm second-stage retrieval on their device.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailAttachmentInfo | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | project NetworkMessageId, FileName, FileType) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails, AttachmentFile = FileName, AttachmentType = FileType, UrlCount
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailAttachmentInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | project NetworkMessageId, FileName, FileType) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails, AttachmentFile = FileName, AttachmentType = FileType, UrlCount
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.src_user="customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com" OR All_Email.src_user="*@9i6pokerdepot.com") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.subject, All_Email.action, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.src_user="customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com" OR All_Email.src_user="*@9i6pokerdepot.com") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.subject, All_Email.action, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | sort - _time
Second-stage BAT dropper retrieval from ClickUp attachment subdomain t90141296286 AIDelivery High
Detects a host resolving/connecting to the campaign-specific ClickUp attachment subdomain t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com that hosted the Financial_report.bat dropper. Anchors on the unique campaign subdomain (not generic ClickUp SaaS traffic) so it does not fire on legitimate ClickUp usage. Rationale: t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com and the URL path fragment fb39c3a9-3161-40ad are the exact stage-2 BAT dropper indicators from the article IOC table; the campaign-unique subdomain avoids FPs from normal ClickUp use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/
ATT&CKT1105 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.All_Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user who legitimately owns ClickUp workspace t90141296286 downloads their own attachment (implausible given campaign attribution)
  • Security analyst detonating the sample in an internet-connected sandbox on a monitored host
  • Web proxy or SWG pre-fetching/scanning the URL from an appliance IP
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling automatically resolving the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host+user and the initiating process for the connection; confirm whether a .bat/.exe file was written (DeviceFileEvents FileOriginUrl containing clickup-attachments.com). 2) Contain: isolate the device, block *.clickup-attachments.com/t90141296286 at the proxy, and revoke the user's active sessions. 3) Hunt: chase the process-tree UC (BAT -> hidden PowerShell -> pixeldrain) and the pixeldrain installer UC on the same host and across the org.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com" or (RemoteUrl has "clickup-attachments.com" and RemoteUrl has "fb39c3a9-3161-40ad")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
